answer.exemplar: The original side chain ended in a charged carboxyl group, so it sat on the wet outer surface where water could reach it. The replacement is a plain hydrocarbon with no charge and no hydroxyl, so that position now presents a water-repelling patch where a charge used to be. In the crowded, dry interior of the red cell that patch locks onto a hydrophobic patch on a neighbouring chain, and the chains polymerise into stiff fibres that bend the cell into a crescent.

questions.explanation: Shape in a folded protein is a consequence of how side chains pack, so replacing one charged surface side chain with a nonpolar one does not simply substitute a small piece; it creates a hydrophobic patch in a place that used to be hydrophilic, and that patch is a new sticky surface. In the crowded, oxygen-poor interior of a red cell the exposed patch binds a matching patch on a neighbouring chain, so the chains polymerise into long stiff fibres that deform the cell. The tempting wrong belief is that a one-letter change is cosmetic, but the whole surface chemistry of the molecule has changed, which is why a heterozygous carrier can be perfectly healthy while two copies of the allele are not.
questions.hint: Ask what the replaced side chain was doing for the folded shape.

questions.explanation: Each of the four chains carries one heme, and each heme holds one iron ion that reversibly binds one oxygen molecule, so the whole four-chain complex carries four. Four chains packed together is quaternary structure, and the arrangement is not a formality: when one oxygen binds, its chain shifts slightly, which raises the affinity of the other three, so the protein loads efficiently in the oxygen-rich lungs and unloads efficiently in the tissues. The tempting wrong belief is that one protein takes one cargo, which is true of a single chain such as myoglobin but not of a tetramer built for cooperative loading.

questions.explanation: Free energy changes add when reactions are coupled, so the total is the sum of the two signed numbers: minus 30.5 plus 25.0 equals minus 5.5 kJ per mole, and because the total is negative the coupled reaction is spontaneous and can drive work such as trapping glucose as glucose-6-phosphate. The check is that hydrolysis releases 30.5 while phosphorylation consumes 25.0, leaving 5.5 to spare, about 18 percent. The tempting wrong belief is that a plus and a minus 5.5 cancel to zero, which would leave nothing to pay for anything; coupling is a budget, and here the budget is in surplus.

questions.explanation: The compact three-dimensional shape of one folded chain is tertiary structure, and it is held together by side chains far apart in the sequence tucking water-hating groups together, by salt bridges and hydrogen bonds, and by covalent disulfide links between cysteines. Primary structure is only the sequence, secondary structure is the local helix and sheet held by backbone bonds, and quaternary structure needs more than one chain, which the stem rules out. The tempting wrong belief is that the biggest contacts must be between nearby residues, but proximity along the chain does not matter at all, which is exactly why distant residues end up touching in the finished fold.

answer.exemplar: ATP is a recyclable intermediate, not a bulk store. Each molecule hydrolysed to do work is rebuilt from ADP and phosphate using energy from glucose and fatty acid oxidation, so the same pool cycles thousands of times a second and its size barely changes. The runner's mass is set by what is burned, not by the ATP that passed through.

questions.explanation: A cell holds only a few grams of ATP at any moment, and every molecule used is rebuilt within seconds from ADP and phosphate using energy from glucose and fatty acid oxidation, so the same few grams circulate again and again like a bucket being refilled rather than a tank being drained. The total mass of ATP made across a race can exceed body weight, yet none of it accumulates, so weight tracks what was burned and what was drunk. The tempting wrong belief is that ATP is a fuel stockpiled like fat, which would mean heavy ATP use should make a runner measurably lighter.
questions.hint: Ask what refills the pool each time a molecule is used.

questions.explanation: The two ends of the range fail for opposite reasons, which is why one shape cannot describe both. At 10 degrees the enzyme is folded correctly but the molecules collide too rarely to react often, and warming restores activity, so the fold is intact. Above about 60 degrees the thermal motion breaks the hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts holding the fold, so activity falls and does not return on cooling, and that is denaturation. The tempting wrong belief is that cold denatures like heat, and it is worth noting the practical exception: cold can still denature some proteins, so the rule is about the usual case, not a law.

questions.explanation: Currency and store differ in how the energy is packaged: a store is built up over time and drawn on when needed, while currency is small, instantly spendable, and constantly recycled. Fat and glycogen are the stores, roughly 9 and 4 kcal per gram, and they are converted into ATP at the rate the cell demands it. The tempting wrong belief is that the molecule holding the most energy must be the one spent on each individual step, but ATP holds less per molecule precisely so it can be handed over in small, controllable amounts, which is why hydrolysis is paired with a specific reaction rather than releasing a flood of heat.

questions.explanation: Adenine and guanine are purines with two fused rings, while thymine and cytosine are pyrimidines with one, so pairing one of each keeps the distance between the two backbones constant no matter which pair is present. A constant width lets every pair stack evenly, which is what makes a long sequence of any composition possible. The reversed 5-prime to 3-prime labels in the diagram matter for the same reason: because the strands run in opposite directions, each pair of bases meets in one consistent geometry. The tempting wrong belief is that two purines could pair fine, but a pair of two-ringed bases would buckle the helix, and a pair of two pyrimidines would let it pinch shut, so both would wreck the uniform spacing.

questions.explanation: Breaking a bond always costs energy, so no energy can be collected from the inside of a bond. About 30.5 kJ per mole is released because the products sit lower in free energy than the reactants: the three adjacent phosphate groups repel each other electrostatically in ATP, and hydrolysis relieves that crowding and leaves ADP and inorganic phosphate better hydrated. The tempting wrong belief is the loaded-spring picture, which also gets the logic of coupling backwards: since hydrolysis on its own would just settle to equilibrium, the cell gets useful work only by linking it to a reaction that is even more negative, such as joining a phosphate to glucose.
questions.hint: Ask whether breaking any bond, in any molecule, ever returns energy.
